title: Green Revolution and Land Reforms

cards.h: Land and food: the base of rural politics
cards.b:
In 1950, about 70% of Indians worked on land, much of it owned by zamindars and cultivated by tenants and landless labourers. Two policies tried to change this: land reforms (redistribute rights) and the Green Revolution (raise output with technology).

The first was about equity, the second about productivity. Both reshaped rural politics: they created a class of owner-farmers who became a political force, and left landless Dalits largely behind.

UPSC asks: Why did land reforms have limited success? What were the political consequences of the Green Revolution? How do these explain today's farm protests?

1. Abolition of intermediaries (zamindari): done in most states in the 1950s. The First Amendment (1951) added Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule to shield these laws from court challenge.
  2. Tenancy reform: security of tenure, fair rent, and ownership for tenants.
  3. Ceilings on landholding and redistribution of surplus land. National guidelines came in 1972.
  4. Consolidation of fragmented holdings, most successful in Punjab, Haryana and western UP.

Land is a State List subject, so results varied widely by state.

• Kerala: the 1957 Communist government began, and the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969 abolished tenancy, giving ownership to tenants from 1970.
  • West Bengal: Operation Barga (from 1978) registered sharecroppers (bargadars) and secured their share.
  • Jammu and Kashmir: the Big Landed Estates Abolition Act (1950) redistributed land without compensation under Sheikh Abdullah.

Common factor: strong peasant movements and Left or reform-minded parties.

Where they failed: in much of north India, landlords used benami transfers, fake partitions and court cases to evade ceilings. Officials and legislators often came from landed castes. Of land declared surplus, only a small fraction (a few million acres nationally) was ever distributed.

Vinoba Bhave's Bhoodan (from 1951) collected pledges of land, but much of it was poor or never distributed.

Francine Frankel, India's Political Economy (1978)

The Congress depended on dominant rural castes to mobilise votes, so it could not push radical reform against them. Planners accommodated rather than confronted.

Daniel Thorner, The Agrarian Prospect in India (1956)

Showed how the reforms were weakened by loopholes and landlord resistance.

P.S. Appu, Land Reforms in India (1996)

A former official's account of the gap between law and implementation.

Atul Kohli, The State and Poverty in India (1987)

Explained West Bengal's success by a disciplined, left-of-centre party with an organised rural base.

After droughts in 1965-66 and dependence on US wheat under PL-480, the government under Agriculture Minister C. Subramaniam adopted a new strategy. Scientist M.S. Swaminathan brought in high-yielding wheat developed by Norman Borlaug in Mexico.

Institutions: the Food Corporation of India and the Agricultural Prices Commission (both 1965; the latter now CACP) for minimum support prices and procurement.

Results: wheat output more than doubled within a few years, and India became self-sufficient in food grains by the 1970s.

• Rise of a farmer class: middle peasants (Jats, Yadavs, Kurmis, Patidars) gained wealth. The Rudolphs called them "bullock capitalists". They became politically assertive.
  • Charan Singh built the Bharatiya Kranti Dal (1967-69) on this base and became PM in 1979.
  • Farmers' movements of the 1980s (Sharad Joshi, Mahendra Singh Tikait) demanded higher prices and cheaper inputs, the "India vs Bharat" argument.
  • Regional inequality: gains concentrated in irrigated north-west regions.
  • Class and caste conflict: landless labourers, often Dalits, gained less. Violence such as the Kilvenmani massacre (Tamil Nadu, 1968) was linked to wage disputes.
  • The Punjab crisis of the 1980s has been linked in part to Green Revolution tensions.

Francine Frankel, India's Green Revolution: Economic Gains and Political Costs (1971), predicted these social tensions.

• Vandana Shiva, The Violence of the Green Revolution (1991): monoculture, chemicals and water use destroyed ecology and fed conflict in Punjab.
  • Groundwater: free power and paddy cultivation have drained aquifers in Punjab and Haryana.
  • Debt and distress: rising input costs and price risk; farmer suicides became a policy issue from the late 1990s.
  • Nutrition: a focus on wheat and rice displaced pulses and millets.

Defence: it ended famine fears, lowered food prices for the poor, and gave India strategic independence. M.S. Swaminathan himself called for an "evergreen revolution" that is productive and sustainable.

• Farm laws 2020 and repeal (November 2021): farmers in Punjab and Haryana, Green Revolution heartlands, feared the end of MSP-based procurement.
  • MSP debate: the National Commission on Farmers (Swaminathan, 2004-06) suggested MSP at cost of production plus 50%. Demands for a legal guarantee continue.
  • Bharat Ratna (2024) for M.S. Swaminathan and Charan Singh, both symbols of this history.
  • Land: the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013; digital land records (DILRMP) and SVAMITVA property cards; Bihar's Bandyopadhyay Land Reforms Commission (2008) report was largely shelved.
  • Crop diversification and millets (UN International Year of Millets, 2023).

Land ownership remains unequal. Agricultural census data show that small and marginal farmers (below 2 hectares) are over 85% of holdings but own under half the area. Dalits remain largely landless.

This links to caste politics: dominant landowning castes (Jats, Marathas, Patidars) now demand OBC quotas as farming becomes less profitable. Land conflicts underlie tribal movements against mining and dams.

Thinkers to connect: Ambedkar argued for state ownership of agricultural land in States and Minorities (1947), as collective farming would end landlessness. His proposal was not adopted.

Structure: context; four stages of land reform; successes (Kerala, West Bengal) and failures; scholars (Frankel, Thorner, Kohli); Green Revolution and its institutions; political impact (bullock capitalists, Charan Singh, farmer movements); ecological critique (Shiva); links to 2020-21 protests; conclusion.
